title: Proactor

validation.research: Six primary sources: the original Pyarali/Harrison/Schmidt/Jordan Proactor paper, Boost.Asio’s Proactor model, Microsoft I/O completion ports, synchronous/asynchronous I/O and CancelIoEx documentation, and Python asyncio platform support. Initiation, operation processing, queued completion, matching handler dispatch, request identity, transferred-byte counts, partial transfers, borrowed buffer lifetime, immediate/submission outcomes, cancellation races, dispatcher concurrency, completion order and admission bounds are explicit. Completion dispatcher is a participant rather than an invented alias. A portable async keyword is not treated as proof of native completion I/O; the Python example is explicitly a deterministic simulation.

Deterministic in-memory model only: no real I/O, OS handles, kernel-borrowed buffers, threads, timers, native API calls, guaranteed cancellation effectiveness, persistent effects, or native performance claim.

example_limits: Original Python 3.11+ deterministic single-thread in-memory simulation. read initiates a request, complete is the manually controlled test-backend terminal-result hook, and dispatch_one consumes a queued result and invokes the matching handler. At most two outstanding requests ask for 1–8 bytes each, including completed requests waiting for dispatch. Each has a separate ordinary bytearray and callback; IDs are scoped correlation values rather than security credentials. Requesting cancellation retains state and can precede a successful, canceled, or failed result. Error results contain no data in this model; zero-byte success models stream EOF, and short reads do not imply a complete business record. Duplicate results are rejected. Dispatch copies bytes, releases pending admission state before invoking the callback, and propagates handler failure without retrying it or discarding other ready results. Callbacks are serialized and all harness queues drain. Slot retention, result/status restrictions, dispatch ordering and accounting are explicit model choices, not native API promises. No real I/O, OS handles, kernel-borrowed buffers, threads, timers, native Windows API execution, durability, effective cancellation mechanism, or native performance claim is inferred.
